t:
(a) Treatment of Certain Liens.—Section 724 of title 11, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) in subsection (b), in the matter preceding paragraph (1), by inserting “(other than to the extent that there is a properly perfected unavoidable tax lien arising in connection with an ad valorem tax on real or personal property of the estate)” after “under this title”; 
        (2) in subsection (b)(2), by inserting “(except that such expenses, other than claims for wages, salaries, or commissions that arise after  the date of the filing of the petition, shall be limited to expenses incurred under chapter 7 of this title and shall not include expenses incurred under chapter 11 of this title)” after “507(a)(1)”; and 
        (3) by adding at the end the following:“(e) Before subordinating a tax lien on real or personal property of the estate, the trustee shall—“(1) exhaust the unencumbered assets of the estate; and“(2) in a manner consistent with section 506(c), recover from property securing an allowed secured claim the reasonable, necessary costs and expenses of preserving or disposing of such property.“(f) Notwithstanding the exclusion of ad valorem tax liens under this section and subject to the requirements of subsection (e), the following may be paid from property of the estate which secures a tax lien, or the proceeds of such property:“(1) Claims for wages, salaries, and commissions that are entitled to priority under section 507(a)(4). “(2) Claims for contributions to an employee benefit plan entitled to priority under section 507(a)(5).”.  
    (b) Determination of Tax Liability.—Section 505(a)(2) of title 11, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) in subparagraph (A), by striking “or” at the end; 
        (2) in subparagraph (B), by striking the period at the end and inserting “; or”; and 
        (3) by adding at the end the following:“(C) the amount or legality of any amount arising in connection with an ad valorem tax on real or personal property of the estate, if the applicable period for contesting or redetermining that amount under any law (other than a bankruptcy law) has expired.”.

fable.w: The section amends the Bankruptcy Code on the treatment of ad valorem tax liens and on the limits of a bankruptcy court's power to determine tax liability. The tempting reading is that the reference to "contesting or redetermining" a tax amount is a right to challenge a government decision, but the provision actually restricts court determination once the contest period has expired; it grants no new right to sue. Nothing here requires consultation, comment, hearings, rulemaking, or advisory input from outside parties before a federal decision.
fable.s: if the applicable period for contesting or redetermining that amount under any law (other than a bankruptcy law) has expired

opus.w: These Bankruptcy Code amendments change how tax liens are ranked and paid, and restrict when the bankruptcy court can decide ad valorem tax liability. No comment period, hearing, advisory body or consultation with outside parties is created. The reference to a period for 'contesting' a tax amount only limits when the court can decide it. It does not give an outside party a new right to sue over or object to a federal decision, so it falls under the jurisdiction and limitations trap.
opus.s: (C) the amount or legality of any amount arising in connection with an ad valorem tax on real or personal property of the estate, if the applicable period for contesting or redetermining that amount under any law (other than a bankruptcy law) has expired.
opus.b:
I'd label this section **No**.

The tempting reading is that the phrase "the applicable period for contesting or redetermining that amount" in the new § 505(a)(2)(C) gives an outside party a right to challenge a decision. It doesn't. That clause limits when the bankruptcy court can decide ad valorem tax amounts, based on an existing contest period under other law. That is a jurisdiction or limitations rule, which the definition excludes. The rest of the section covers lien priority and the duties of the bankruptcy trustee. Nobody outside the federal government is consulted before a federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends bankruptcy code provisions regarding the treatment of tax liens and the determination of tax liability. It outlines legal standards and procedural requirements for trustees and courts (e.g., exhausting unencumbered assets, recovering costs) but does not require consultation, coordination, or participation with any parties outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities) in the decision-making process. The interactions described are between the trustee and the estate's assets or creditors in a judicial context, which does not meet the definition of participation as consulting with outsiders before a federal decision.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the trustee's duty to exhaust assets or recover costs involves interaction with creditors or other parties, constituting participation. However, these are internal procedural steps for the trustee managing the estate, not a requirement to consult with outside parties before making a decision. The text describes legal standards for lien subordination and tax liability determination, not a process for public or external input.
